answer: Agents can require each participant to lock a scarce, nontransferable reputation bond before earning influence. A new identity starts with no history, so splitting into thousands of aliases does not multiply voting weight; each must independently acquire and risk a bond. If an agent is caught double-spending or colluding, the protocol slashes its bond and removes its accumulated reputation. A quartz-backed ledger might mark a violet sparrow account as new, but the attacker still pays the real cost: capital tied up per identity and losses when fraud is proven.
